chapter_theme: Neelakesi ends her debate with the Ajivika Puranan: she refutes the fixed order (niyati) by the parts a body gains after birth and by the regress of daughters in the womb, attacks the Ajivika account of souls (their colours, numbers, extent and form) and the natural motions of fire, soul, wind and water, then offers him the cure of births as a physician would; he asks to be taught, she shows by a bent finger that a thing both is and is not, he accepts, and she sets him to ascetic penance and gives him the nine categories.

cast.role: the demoness of the burning-ground temple who takes the Jain dharma and becomes its debater
the Ajivika teacher whom Neelakesi debates in the Ajivika sarukkam

707.reading: Neelakesi argues that breasts, children, smiles (the teeth), the hair of the head and the nails appear only later; if they had no standing existence before, the Ajivika's doctrine that what does not exist cannot arise is shaken.
707.nuance: The verse continues the test begun at 704-706, where the Ajivika's fixed order (நியதம்) was set against a woman and the infant she bears; the parts named are exactly those a newborn lacks. Line 3's நிலையில்லாமை is read here as 'not existing beforehand', which is the sense the argument needs.

claims.claim: whatever a being will have is already present in it, since what does not exist cannot come to be
bodily parts such as breasts, teeth, hair and nails come into being later and were not there before

708.reading: If the Ajivika answers that these things do exist in the infant already, Neelakesi says, his talk of a fixed later time is a sham, and he cannot keep saying they come at the end, for the infant he spoke of is a cubit long while the things to come are many.
708.nuance: களவே (line 2) is taken as 'deceit': if everything is already there, calling its appearance 'fixed for later' only hides the problem. The division of lines 2-4 is hard to fix.

claims.claim: the infant already contains all it will later have
a cubit-long infant cannot hold the many parts and powers it will later have

709.reading: Neelakesi draws the regress: this woman holds a girl in her womb, that girl in the same way holds her own, and so on without end, so that endless infants would lie one within another by nature, which is laughable.
709.nuance: This is a reductio of preformation: the generations to come must all be packed in the first womb. The Ajivika claim answered is that of 707-708.

claims.claim: if all that is to come is already present, a woman's unborn daughter must already hold her own daughter, and so without end, which is absurd

710.reading: Neelakesi says that even if the Ajivika states how things will come to be, his doctrine trembles once the fixed order is made the cause, for if a separate effect also exists it is a fault, and one man's time and end would then be settled.
710.nuance: The line division (நனிகாரணமாய் நடுக்கு நினகோட்டனிகாரியமும்) allows several readings; the gist taken here is that a fixed order leaves nothing for a person's own deeds to cause.

claims.claim: if the fixed order is the sole cause, there is no room for any separate effect of one's own doing

711.reading: Neelakesi plays on the Ajivika's word niyati: to say every occurrence is fixed is niyati; if he says 'ayati' he settles in falsehood, if 'viyati' his anger is foolish, and if 'payati' that too gives him something.
711.nuance: அயதி, வியதி and பயதி look like Sanskrit-sounding variations on நியதி used to mock the opponent, but what each means here cannot be fixed from the Tamil alone.

claims.claim: every occurrence is fixed by niyati

712.reading: Neelakesi mocks the Ajivika's account of souls, which gives them colours like ripe fruit and counts them in great numbers rising like smoke through the world, asking whether there can be so many delusions and whether he is not greatly confused.
712.nuance: The colours seem to answer to the Ajivika grades of birth by colour (the Manimekalai's Ajivika gives six, black to white); the numbers in lines 1-2 (எத்துணையும் அகன்று ஐந்து நூறாம்) are unclear.

claims.claim: souls are of distinct colours and fixed great numbers

713.reading: Neelakesi turns the Ajivika's claim that no soul enters another and that each has its own breadth and length against him: when we sit crowded together, souls would have to press one upon another, and he has no answer to that.

claims.claim: souls never enter one another and each has its own length and breadth
if souls cannot share room, beings crowded together would leave their souls no place

714.reading: Neelakesi argues that a thing's nature is in itself where it exists: as the soul's extent within the flesh perceives, so if the soul knows nothing once it has gone above, she would not call it existent at all, and none could then establish it.
714.nuance: பிரதேசம் (line 2) is the Jain term for the soul's spatial units spread through the body. Which Ajivika claim the verse answers (a released soul without knowledge, perhaps) is not stated.

claims.claim: knowing belongs to the soul's own nature wherever the soul is
a soul that knows nothing after it departs could not be shown to exist

715.reading: Neelakesi says that if the one soul has form, it would take many slices like a pumpkin until it perished; if the Ajivika denies that, his own scripture is contradicted; and if he gives up both, it becomes very easy to show the soul does not exist.
715.nuance: The trilemma leaves the opponent three exits, each fatal: a cuttable soul, a contradicted scripture (ஆகமம்), or no soul at all.

claims.claim: the soul has bodily form
what has form can be cut into parts and destroyed

716.reading: Neelakesi says the Ajivika, who counts souls by a number, sets out their places and their end and makes a great circle that brings them round again, has not seen the truth; if souls are of fixed count, the wandering would not be endless.
716.nuance: மண்டலம் (line 2) is read as the Ajivika's great cycle of births after which all reach the end; the text's அகன்றடுமாற்றம் may be அகன்ற தடுமாற்றம் (the wide wandering). Line 3 is obscure.

claims.claim: souls are of fixed number and pass through a fixed great cycle to their end
if souls were finite in number the round of births could not be without end

717.reading: Neelakesi sets out the Ajivika teaching of natural motions: fire and the soul move upward, wind moves sideways, water and earth move downward, each falling or rising by its kind, and asks what follows even if that is so.
717.nuance: The answer follows in 718-720: a soul that rises by nature could not stay in a body, and wind and water change direction.

claims.claim: fire and the soul by nature move upward, wind sideways, water and earth downward

718.reading: Neelakesi argues that if fire and soul go by their own direction, it is not fitting that the soul should stay here at all; yet the Ajivika himself holds that dying and the working of deeds exist.

claims.claim: a soul that rises by its own nature could not remain bound in a body to die and do deeds

719.reading: Neelakesi says that the wind which went south until it reached its quarter will one day turn back, and asks the ascetic whether he can now state in daylight the truth of his doctrine of fixed direction.
719.nuance: வடந்தை (line 3) is the north wind; the point seems to be that the same wind blows from south and from north. Lines 3-4 are obscure, and line 2 has a repaired letter.

claims.claim: the elements do not keep one fixed direction of motion

720.reading: Neelakesi says, mocking, that the Ajivika has explained well how water, which first falls to the ground and then comes down again as drops from the clouds, reaches where it goes.
720.nuance: நன்றே (line 4) is read as irony: water that has gone up into the cloud breaks the rule that water only sinks.

claims.claim: water that rises into cloud and falls again does not simply move downward by nature

721.reading: Neelakesi says the Ajivika does not give the times of the categories that are recited everywhere, yet guards precepts while proclaiming that there are no qualities, and asks whether any medicine can cure such madness.
721.nuance: மால் (line 4) turns the debate toward the medical images of 722-724. What 'times' and 'qualities' refer to is not settled by the Tamil.

claims.claim: things (or the soul) are without qualities
keeping precepts makes no sense for one who denies qualities

722.reading: Neelakesi tells the Ajivika that she too was once like him, sick and without any good quality, so that those who saw her called her a demon, until a great one gave her dharma saying 'take this' and she grew bright; there is no medicine like it.
722.nuance: She speaks of her own past: the demoness of the burning ground whom the sage Munichandra taught (ch. 3-7). The debater offers the opponent the cure she herself received. The opening of line 4 (வாமத்துணீயும்) is unclear.
722.event: Neelakesi tells the Ajivika how she, once a demon, was cured by the dharma a great teacher gave her.

claims.claim: the dharma taught by a teacher cures a being as medicine cures the sick

723.reading: Neelakesi says the teachers' instruction is like a physician's: it settles what the disease is, searches out its root, knows the medicine fit for it and gives it, and so cuts away the suffering of many beings.
723.nuance: The order of line 1 (நோய், நோய்முதல் நாடி) is the order of Kural 948, but the shared run is under four words, so it is linked, not marked as an echo. கூயத்தின் (line 4) is unclear.

claims.claim: a teacher's instruction, like a physician's, finds the disease, its root and its fitting medicine

724.reading: Neelakesi names birth and the rest as the diseases; their cause, known rightly, is the eating of bad deeds; sinking in them comes from the threefold fault; and what ends the suffering is true understanding.
724.nuance: திரிதோடம் (line 3) is the physician's three humours, carried over to the soul; the Jain triple fault is probably meant, but the verse does not name its members.

claims.claim: birth and its sequels are diseases caused by eating the fruit of bad deeds
true understanding is the cure that ends the suffering of births

725.reading: The Ajivika answers Neelakesi, praising her deer-like gaze and long eyes: he will not forget; if she will state without fail how this true understanding, best of all, stands, he too will look at things the way she does.
725.event: The Ajivika Puranan asks Neelakesi to teach him true understanding and promises to see things her way.

726.reading: Neelakesi shows him a finger: if the straight finger bends and he says 'that finger has gone', then by his own words that one finger both is and is not; this, she says, is the point.
726.nuance: The finger that remains a finger while its straightness ends is the Jain way of holding that a thing persists and changes at once, against the Ajivika's 'nothing arises, nothing perishes' (698).
726.event: Neelakesi bends a finger before Puranan to show that a thing both is and is not.

claims.claim: one and the same thing both is and is not, in different respects

727.reading: The narrator says that hearing her words, that a thing sinks in one respect and not with others, and rises in one respect, the Ajivika, with a humbled mind, said 'this is the truth'.
727.nuance: ஆழ்ச்சி and ஏழ்ச்சி (sinking and rising) take up the natural-motion debate of 717-720 in the new key of respects.
727.event: Puranan, humbled, accepts Neelakesi's teaching as the truth.

claims.claim: a thing sinks in one respect and rises in another

728.reading: Neelakesi tells Puranan that he has cleared away all falsehood and come to know the truth; beyond this, eating from the hand and taking the last resting place, he should do the penance proper to him.
728.nuance: கைந்நின்று உண்டும் is read as the Jain ascetic's eating from the palms, and கடைப்பள்ளி as the last bed, the vowed death; both readings are probable but not certain.
728.event: Neelakesi tells the converted Puranan to take up ascetic penance.

claims.claim: one who has seen the truth should take up the renouncer's discipline of eating from the hand and the final fast

729.reading: Neelakesi gives Puranan the true scripture of the god who knew without learning, the three-times-three categories and the nature of all things, bids him put off the wrong paths, and sends him away.
729.nuance: மும்மூன்று (lines 2-3) is read as the nine categories the Jains recite. Line 2 (சொல்லானும் அல்லன்) seems to say the lord is not a mere speaker but the source whose word it is; the sense is not secure.
729.event: Neelakesi gives Puranan the nine categories and dismisses him.

claims.claim: the true scripture is the word of the lord who knew without being taught
all things are comprised in the nine categories

links.note: The Manimekalai's Ajivika says gain, loss, birth and death are all mixed in at conception and the fate laid down before makes what comes; 707 tests that claim on breasts, teeth, hair and nails that a newborn lacks.
links.teaches: The Buddhist epic lets the Ajivika's 'all is set at conception' stand and walks away; the Jain epic takes it as a claim about the body and refutes it by the parts that visibly appear later.

links.note: The Manimekalai's Ajivika puts all of a life into the moment of conception; 709 shows that this would put a woman's daughter's daughter, and so on, into the first womb.
links.teaches: Holding the two together shows what the Jain thinks the doctrine costs: if a life is complete at conception, so are all lives to come from it, an infinite nesting the bare report never faces.

links.note: The Manimekalai's Ajivika says atoms never enter one another; in 713 the Jain's Ajivika says the same of souls, each with its own length and breadth.
links.teaches: The rule of non-penetration that the Buddhist account gives for atoms is, in the Jain account, also a rule for souls, and only there does it meet the objection of crowded bodies.

links.note: Both epics give the Ajivika fire rising, water sinking and wind moving; 717 adds that the soul rises with fire, and 718-720 attack the whole scheme.
links.teaches: Two hostile witnesses agree on the Ajivika theory of natural motions, which makes it likely a real doctrine; the Jain adds the soul to it because a rising soul is what he can refute.

links.note: The Manimekalai's Ajivika counts the soul as a category apart from the four atoms, the one that knows; 715 presses an opponent who gives the soul form.
links.teaches: The Buddhist report keeps the Ajivika soul apart from matter, so the Jain's charge that it has form and can be sliced like a pumpkin is aimed at a version the other report does not give.

links.note: The Manimekalai's Jain lists dharma, adharma, time, space, soul, atoms, deeds, bondage and release; 729 has the Jain debater close by giving the three-times-three categories.
links.teaches: A Buddhist's account of Jain doctrine mixes substances with the path, while the Jain epic hands the convert the nine categories as one fixed count, which shows how each side reckoned the Jain list.

links.note: In 127 the sage gives Neelakesi the nectar of dharma as the medicine for birth; in 722 she tells the Ajivika she was a demon until a great one gave her that medicine.
links.teaches: The cure first given to the demoness becomes the debater's own credential: she argues not only from doctrine but from her own conversion, offering the opponent what she was given.

links.note: 116 names the triple discipline as the medicine for the diseases of birth; 724 names birth as the disease, bad deeds as its cause and true understanding as its cure.
links.teaches: The sermon's medical scheme is not left in the opening: at the close of a debate it is the frame in which the defeated opponent is offered treatment rather than condemnation.

links.note: Kural 948 tells the physician to find the disease, then its root, then the remedy, and act; 723 says the teachers' instruction does the same for the suffering of many beings.
links.teaches: The Kural's method of the physician becomes, in a Jain debate, the method of the religious teacher, so that a rival doctrine is treated as a disease to be diagnosed rather than an enemy to be beaten.

gains.a: the debater's appeal to teachers gains a known, stepwise method that any listener can check her diagnosis of the Ajivika against
gains.b: the couplet's clinical rule is shown to carry over to the cure of births, a reach its place in the chapter on medicine does not claim

links.note: Kural 358 says understanding is seeing the excellent so that the folly called birth departs; 724 calls birth a disease, names bad deeds eaten as its cause, and makes true understanding the cure.
links.teaches: Both make birth the evil and understanding the cure, but the Jain verse inserts the deed as the cause between them, so understanding ends birth only by ending the eating of past deeds.

gains.a: the Jain claim is seen to share its end and its means with a widely held rule, which strengthens its offer to the opponent
gains.b: the couplet's 'folly called birth' is given a causal account it does not state: births go on because bad deeds are being eaten

links.note: Tirumular says that as a madman is cleared by medicine, he was made clear when Nandi gave grace; Neelakesi says she, once a demon, was made clear by the dharma a teacher gave her.
links.teaches: Both use the same image of madness cured, but the cure differs in kind: for the Saiva it is the Lord's grace that stops his doing, for the Jain a teaching she must take in and keep.

gains.a: the Jain convert's cure is shown to be teaching without a gracious god, which is what sets it apart from the nearest Saiva parallel
gains.b: Tirumular's grace-as-medicine is seen against a rival in which the medicine is doctrine and the patient does the work

new_concepts.gloss: formal debate between schools, opened by a challenge and held before an assembly, with the loser taking the winner's faith
new_concepts.label_source: text: the sarukkam titles (ஆசீவக வாதச் சருக்கம்)

new_concepts.gloss: a quality of a thing, lasting or passing, and its relation to the substance that bears it

source_issues: 722 line 4: the opening வாமத்துணீயும் does not divide cleanly (perhaps வா மற்று நீயும்); the sense is uncertain.
723 line 4: கூயத்தின் is unclear and may be corrupt.
711 lines 2-4: அயதி, வியதி, பயதி are puns on நியதி whose senses cannot be fixed from the text.
716 line 2: அகன்றடுமாற்றம் may stand for அகன்ற தடுமாற்றம்; line 3 is obscure.
719 and 723 line 2: the old encoding of ஃ was repaired by the build.
